articles.title: Characteristic roots of $\rho(g)$ are $|G|$-th roots of unity
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a
representation of a finite group $G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, and let
$g \in G$. Every root $\mu$ of the characteristic polynomial of the matrix of $\rho(g)$ in a fixed
basis of $V$ satisfies $\mu^{|G|} = 1$.

articles.title: Character of the dual representation
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a representation of a finite group
$G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, and let $\rho^*$ be its dual representation.
For every $g \in G$, the character of $\rho^*$ at $g$ is the complex conjugate of the character of
$\rho$ at $g$: $\chi_{\rho^*}(g) = \overline{\chi_\rho(g)}$.

articles.title: Character values at inverses are complex conjugates
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a representation of a
finite group $G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, with character $\chi_\rho$.
For every $g \in G$, $\chi_\rho(g^{-1}) = \overline{\chi_\rho(g)}$.

articles.title: Parseval / sum-of-squares for characters
articles.statement:
If `χ` is a combination
of the characters of pairwise non-equivalent irreducible representations
with coefficients `n i`, then the self-pairing of `χ` is the sum of the
squares of the coefficients. In particular, for a single irreducible
`ρ`, taking `χ = χ_ρ` gives self-pairing `1`, and for the regular
character the formula recovers `∑ (dim ρ_i) ^ 2 = |G|` once the regular
character is expanded in irreducibles.

articles.title: Class inner product
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $k$ a field in which $|G|$ is
invertible. For functions $f_1, f_2 \colon G \to k$, their class inner product is
$\langle f_1, f_2 \rangle = |G|^{-1} \sum_{g \in G} f_1(g) f_2(g^{-1})$.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of $\rho(g)$ are $|G|$-th roots of unity
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a representation of a
finite group $G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, and let $g \in G$. Every
eigenvalue $\mu$ of $\rho(g)$ satisfies $\mu^{|G|} = 1$.

This follows because the order of $g$ divides $|G|$.

articles.title: Eigenvalues of $\rho(g)$ are roots of unity of order dividing that of $g$
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a
representation of a finite group $G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, let
$g \in G$, and let $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ be the order of $g$. Every eigenvalue $\mu$ of $\rho(g)$
satisfies $\mu^{\operatorname{ord}(g)} = 1$.

The minimal polynomial of $\rho(g)$ divides $X^{\operatorname{ord}(g)} - 1$, and $\mu$ is a root of
the minimal polynomial.

articles.title: Character criterion for irreducibility
articles.statement:
A finite-dimensional
representation `σ` of a finite group over an algebraically closed field of
characteristic zero is irreducible if and only if the self-pairing of its
character is `1`.

articles.title: Sum of squares of the Wedderburn block sizes
articles.statement:
If `|G|` is nonzero in
an algebraically closed field, the group algebra of a finite group is a product
of matrix algebras with nonzero block sizes whose squares sum to `|G|`.

articles.title: Dimension of an irreducible representation divides the group order
articles.statement:
If `ρ` is an irreducible representation of a finite group `G` over an
algebraically closed field `k` of characteristic zero, then
`dim_k ρ ∣ |G|`. In particular, over `ℂ`, every irreducible degree divides
the order of the group.

articles.title: Maschke's theorem
articles.statement:
Every finite-dimensional complex representation $\sigma$ of a finite
group is equivalent to the direct sum of a finite family of irreducible subrepresentations of
$\sigma$.

articles.title: Every homomorphism of a finite abelian group to the complex numbers is a simple character
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and let $\varphi : G \to \mathbb{C}$ be a monoid homomorphism.
Then there is a simple finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$ whose character
equals $\varphi$.

Proof: Let each $g \in G$ act on the one-dimensional space $\mathbb{C}$ by the scalar
$\varphi(g)$; its trace is $\varphi(g)$. One-dimensional modules are simple. Wikipedia,
“Representation theory of finite groups”, notes that the irreducible characters of an abelian
group are its homomorphisms to $\mathbb{C}^\times$.

## Sources

- J.-P. Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, GTM 42, Ch. I (one-dimensional representations from characters).

articles.title: Characters of simple representations of a finite abelian group are homomorphisms
articles.statement:
Let $G$
be a finite abelian group and let $V$ be a simple finite-dimensional complex representation of
$G$. Then there is a monoid homomorphism $\varphi : G \to \mathbb{C}$ such that the character of
$V$ equals $\varphi$.

Proof: Simplicity of $V$ makes it irreducible, and complex irreducible representations of an
abelian group are one-dimensional (the corollary in Wikipedia, “Schur's lemma”), so $V$ is
one-dimensional. Endomorphisms of a one-dimensional space are scalars, and their traces give the
multiplicative character.

## Sources

- J.-P. Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, GTM 42, §2.8 (degree-one characters of abelian groups).

articles.title: Characters determine simple representations of a finite abelian group
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite
abelian group and let $V$ and $W$ be simple finite-dimensional complex representations of $G$,
with characters $\chi_V$ and $\chi_W$. If $\chi_V = \chi_W$, then $V$ and $W$ are isomorphic.

Proof: For functions $\chi, \psi : G \to \mathbb{C}$ write
$\langle \chi, \psi \rangle = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \chi(g)\,\psi(g^{-1})$, where $|G|$ is
the order of $G$. The orthonormality of irreducible characters gives
$\langle \chi_V, \chi_V \rangle = 1$. Replacing the second character by the equal character
$\chi_W$ gives $\langle \chi_V, \chi_W \rangle = 1$, which forces $V \cong W$. This is the
orthonormality of irreducible characters in Wikipedia, “Character theory”.

## Sources

- J.-P. Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, GTM 42, §2.8 (characters determine representations of abelian groups).

articles.title: The character of a simple representation as a monoid homomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an
algebraically closed field, let $G$ be a commutative monoid, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional
representation of $G$ over $k$ that is simple as an object of the category of finite-dimensional
representations of $G$ over $k$. The character $\chi_V : G \to k$ of $V$, where $\chi_V(g)$ is the
trace of the action of $g$ on $V$, satisfies $\chi_V(1) = 1$ and $\chi_V(gh) = \chi_V(g)\,\chi_V(h)$
for all $g, h \in G$; this is $\chi_V$ regarded as a monoid homomorphism from $G$ to $k$.

articles.title: Characters of simple representations of commutative monoids are multiplicative
articles.statement:
Let $k$
be an algebraically closed field, let $G$ be a commutative monoid, and let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$ that is simple as an object of the category of
finite-dimensional representations of $G$ over $k$. Let $\chi_V : G \to k$ be the character of
$V$, where $\chi_V(g)$ is the trace of the action of $g$ on $V$. Then
$\chi_V(gh) = \chi_V(g)\,\chi_V(h)$ for all $g, h \in G$.

articles.title: The character homomorphism has the character as its underlying function
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an
algebraically closed field, let $G$ be a commutative monoid, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional
representation of $G$ over $k$ that is simple as an object of the category of finite-dimensional
representations of $G$ over $k$. The character of $V$, regarded as a monoid homomorphism from $G$
to $k$, has the character $\chi_V : G \to k$ of $V$ as its underlying function, where $\chi_V(g)$
is the trace of the action of $g$ on $V$.

articles.title: Simple finite-dimensional representations of commutative monoids are one-dimensional
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $G$ be a commutative monoid. Every
finite-dimensional representation $V$ of $G$ over $k$ that is simple as an object of the category
of finite-dimensional representations of $G$ over $k$ has dimension $1$ over $k$.

articles.title: Simple finite-dimensional representations of a monoid are irreducible
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
field and let $G$ be a monoid. If a finite-dimensional representation $V$ of $G$ over $k$ is
simple as an object of the category of finite-dimensional representations of $G$ over $k$, then
$V$ is irreducible as a representation: $V \ne 0$, and the only subrepresentations of $V$ are $0$
and $V$.

articles.title: The action in the one-dimensional representation of a homomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field,
let $G$ be a monoid, let $\varphi : G \to k$ be a monoid homomorphism, and let $k_\varphi$ be the
one-dimensional representation of $G$ on $k$ defined by $\varphi$. For every $g \in G$, the action
of $g$ on $k_\varphi$ is $\varphi(g)$ times the identity map of $k$.

articles.title: The character of the representation of a homomorphism is the homomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
field, let $G$ be a monoid, let $\varphi : G \to k$ be a monoid homomorphism, and let $k_\varphi$
be the one-dimensional representation of $G$ on $k$ in which each $g \in G$ acts by multiplication
by $\varphi(g)$. The character of $k_\varphi$ is $\varphi$: the trace of the action of each
$g \in G$ on $k_\varphi$ is $\varphi(g)$.

articles.title: The representation of a homomorphism is one-dimensional
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be
a monoid, let $\varphi : G \to k$ be a monoid homomorphism, and let $k_\varphi$ be the
representation of $G$ on $k$ in which each $g \in G$ acts by multiplication by $\varphi(g)$. Then
$k_\varphi$ has dimension $1$ over $k$.

articles.title: The representation of a homomorphism is simple
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be a monoid,
let $\varphi : G \to k$ be a monoid homomorphism, and let $k_\varphi$ be the one-dimensional
representation of $G$ on $k$ in which each $g \in G$ acts by multiplication by $\varphi(g)$. Then
$k_\varphi$ is a simple object of the category of finite-dimensional representations of $G$ over
$k$.

articles.title: The one-dimensional representation of a homomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be a
monoid, and let $\varphi : G \to k$ be a monoid homomorphism. This is the finite-dimensional
representation $k_\varphi$ of $G$ on the one-dimensional space $k$ in which each $g \in G$ acts by
multiplication by $\varphi(g)$, that is, by the linear map $x \mapsto \varphi(g)\,x$.

articles.title: Simple representations of commutative monoids act by scalars
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an
algebraically closed field, $G$ a monoid with commutative multiplication, and $V$ a simple
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$ (a simple object of the category of
finite-dimensional representations), with action $\rho$ and character
$\chi_V(g) = \operatorname{tr} \rho(g)$. Then for every $g \in G$ the map $\rho(g)$ is scalar
multiplication by $\chi_V(g)$, that is, $\rho(g) = \chi_V(g) \cdot \mathrm{id}_V$.

articles.title: Schur's lemma, dimension form
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $k$ an algebraically closed
field, and $\rho$, $\sigma$ irreducible representations of $G$ on finite-dimensional $k$-vector
spaces. Then the space $\operatorname{Hom}_G(\rho, \sigma)$ of intertwining maps from $\rho$ to
$\sigma$ has dimension $1$ over $k$ if $\sigma$ and $\rho$ are equivalent, and dimension $0$
otherwise.

articles.title: Multiplicity equals the dimension of the intertwining space
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group,
$k$ an algebraically closed field, and $(\rho_i)_{i \in I}$ a family, indexed by a finite set $I$,
of irreducible representations of $G$ on finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces that are pairwise
non-equivalent: $\rho_i$ and $\rho_j$ are not equivalent whenever $i \ne j$. Let $\sigma$ be a
representation of $G$ on a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $(d_i)_{i \in I}$ be
natural numbers such that $\sigma$ is equivalent to the direct sum of $d_i$ copies of $\rho_i$ over
all $i \in I$. Then for every $i \in I$, $d_i$ equals the dimension over $k$ of the space
$\operatorname{Hom}_G(\rho_i, \sigma)$ of intertwining maps from $\rho_i$ to $\sigma$.

articles.title: Algebra map of a Wedderburn block
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, $G$ a finite
group whose order is nonzero in $k$, and $e \colon k[G] \to \prod_{j < n} M_{d_j}(k)$ an
isomorphism of $k$-algebras from the group algebra onto a product of full matrix algebras. For
$i < n$, this is the $k$-algebra homomorphism $k[G] \to \operatorname{End}_k(k^{d_i})$ that sends
$a \in k[G]$ to the linear map $v \mapsto e(a)_i \, v$, where $e(a)_i$ is the $i$-th component of
$e(a)$.

articles.title: Wedderburn blocks are irreducible
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, $G$ a finite
group whose order is nonzero in $k$, and $e \colon k[G] \to \prod_{j < n} M_{d_j}(k)$ an
isomorphism of $k$-algebras from the group algebra $k[G]$ onto a product of full matrix algebras
$M_{d_j}(k)$ of $d_j \times d_j$ matrices over $k$. For every $i < n$ with $d_i \ne 0$, the
representation of $G$ on $k^{d_i}$ in which $g \in G$ acts by $v \mapsto e(g)_i \, v$, where $g$
is viewed as an element of $k[G]$ and $e(g)_i$ is the $i$-th component of $e(g)$, is
irreducible.

articles.title: Representation of a Wedderburn block
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, $G$ a
finite group whose order is nonzero in $k$, and $e \colon k[G] \to \prod_{j < n} M_{d_j}(k)$ an
isomorphism of $k$-algebras from the group algebra $k[G]$ onto a product of full matrix algebras
$M_{d_j}(k)$ of $d_j \times d_j$ matrices over $k$. For $i < n$, this is the representation of $G$
on $k^{d_i}$ in which $g \in G$ acts by $v \mapsto e(g)_i \, v$, where $g$ is viewed as an element
of $k[G]$ and $e(g)_i$ is the $i$-th component of $e(g)$.

articles.title: Direct-sum isomorphism in group homology and the first projection
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
commutative ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$ representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
and write $H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group homology of a representation $M$. The isomorphism
$H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ followed by the projection onto $H_n(G, A)$
equals the map $H_n(G, A \oplus B) \to H_n(G, A)$ induced by the projection $A \oplus B \to A$.

articles.title: Direct-sum isomorphism in group homology and the second projection
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
commutative ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$ representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
and write $H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group homology of a representation $M$. The isomorphism
$H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ followed by the projection onto $H_n(G, B)$
equals the map $H_n(G, A \oplus B) \to H_n(G, B)$ induced by the projection $A \oplus B \to B$.

articles.title: Forward map of the direct-sum isomorphism in group homology
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a commutative
ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$ representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write
$H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group homology of a representation $M$. The forward map of the
isomorphism $H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ is the map into the biproduct
whose components are the maps $H_n(G, A \oplus B) \to H_n(G, A)$ and
$H_n(G, A \oplus B) \to H_n(G, B)$ induced by the projections $A \oplus B \to A$ and
$A \oplus B \to B$.

articles.title: Direct-sum isomorphism in group homology and the first inclusion
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
commutative ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$ representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
and write $H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group homology of a representation $M$. The inclusion of
$H_n(G, A)$ into $H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ followed by the inverse of the isomorphism
$H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ equals the map
$H_n(G, A) \to H_n(G, A \oplus B)$ induced by the inclusion $A \to A \oplus B$.

articles.title: Direct-sum isomorphism in group homology and the second inclusion
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
commutative ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$ representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
and write $H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group homology of a representation $M$. The inclusion of
$H_n(G, B)$ into $H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ followed by the inverse of the isomorphism
$H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ equals the map
$H_n(G, B) \to H_n(G, A \oplus B)$ induced by the inclusion $B \to A \oplus B$.

articles.title: Inverse map of the direct-sum isomorphism in group homology
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a commutative
ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$ representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write
$H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group homology of a representation $M$. The inverse map of the
isomorphism $H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ is the map out of the biproduct
whose components are the maps $H_n(G, A) \to H_n(G, A \oplus B)$ and
$H_n(G, B) \to H_n(G, A \oplus B)$ induced by the inclusions $A \to A \oplus B$ and
$B \to A \oplus B$.

articles.title: Group homology of a direct sum
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a group, $A$ and $B$
representations of $G$ over $k$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write $H_n(G, M)$ for the $n$th group
homology of a representation $M$. This is the isomorphism
$H_n(G, A \oplus B) \cong H_n(G, A) \oplus H_n(G, B)$ obtained by applying the $n$th group homology
functor, which is additive, to the biproduct $A \oplus B$.

## Sources

- NumberTheoryI, Section 23.4, Corollary 23.22.

articles.title: Invariance of group cohomology under group isomorphism
articles.statement: Group cohomology is invariant under group isomorphism.

articles.title: Finiteness hypothesis for the Herbrand quotient
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a
commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$. The representation $M$ satisfies
the Herbrand finiteness hypothesis when its Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and
$\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are both finite.

articles.title: Herbrand quotients agree when Tate cohomology in degrees $0$ and $-1$ is in bijection
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$, $N$ two $R$-linear representations
of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$, $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$, $\hat H^0(G, N)$ and
$\hat H^{-1}(G, N)$ are finite. If there are bijections between the underlying sets of
$\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^0(G, N)$ and between those of $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ and
$\hat H^{-1}(G, N)$, then the Herbrand quotients of $M$ and $N$ are equal.

articles.title: The denominator of the Herbrand quotient is nonzero
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a
commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups
$\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the number of elements of
$\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ is nonzero.

articles.title: The denominator of the Herbrand quotient is positive
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a
commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups
$\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the number of elements of
$\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ is positive.

articles.title: Herbrand quotient as a ratio of orders
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative
ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$
and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the Herbrand quotient of $M$ equals the rational number
$|\hat H^0(G, M)| / |\hat H^{-1}(G, M)|$, where $|X|$ is the number of elements of $X$.

articles.title: Positivity of the Herbrand quotient
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring
and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and
$\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the Herbrand quotient of $M$ is strictly positive.

articles.title: Herbrand quotient
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an
$R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and
$\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. The Herbrand quotient of $M$ is the rational number
$h(M) = |\hat H^0(G, M)| / |\hat H^{-1}(G, M)|$, where $|X|$ is the number of elements of $X$.

articles.title: Periodicity of Tate cohomology for finite cyclic groups
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring,
$G$ a finite cyclic group and $A$ a representation of $G$ over $R$. Then for every integer $n$,
the Tate cohomology groups $\hat{H}^n(G, A)$ and $\hat{H}^{n+2}(G, A)$ are isomorphic as
$R$-modules.

articles.title: Cardinality of finite Tate cohomology as a natural number
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$
a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ and $n$ an integer such that the Tate
cohomology group $\hat H^n(G, M)$ is finite. Then the cardinality of $\hat H^n(G, M)$ equals its
number of elements, a natural number viewed as a cardinal number.

articles.title: Cardinality of Tate cohomology
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring, $M$ an
$R$-linear representation of $G$ and $n$ an integer. This is the cardinality of the Tate
cohomology group $\hat H^n(G, M)$, as a cardinal number (possibly infinite).

articles.title: Cardinality of Tate homology in degree zero
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative
ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$. The cardinality of the degree-$0$ Tate homology
of $M$ equals the cardinality of the Tate cohomology group $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$.

The cardinality of Tate homology in degree $n$ is defined as that of $\hat H^{-n-1}(G, M)$, so
this holds by definition.

articles.title: Cardinality of Tate homology
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring
and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$. For an integer $n$, the cardinality $h_n(M)$
of the degree-$n$ Tate homology of $M$ is defined as the cardinal number of the Tate
cohomology group $\hat H^{-n-1}(G, M)$, following the convention $\hat H_n = \hat H^{-n-1}$.

articles.title: Groups with exactly one irreducible representation of each dimension
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has
exactly one irreducible complex representation of each dimension when for every $n \ge 1$ there
is an irreducible homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and any two irreducible
homomorphisms $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ are equivalent. Representations are arbitrary
homomorphisms of the abstract group $G$; no continuity is required.

articles.title: Equivalent representations into $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group. Two
homomorphisms $\rho, \sigma \colon G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ are equivalent when there is a
matrix $P \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ with $\sigma(g) = P \rho(g) P^{-1}$ for all $g \in G$.

articles.title: Irreducible representations into $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group and
$\rho \colon G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ a homomorphism. Then $\rho$ is irreducible when
$n \ge 1$ and the only subspaces $W$ of $\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\rho(g)v \in W$ for all $g \in G$ and
$v \in W$ are $0$ and $\mathbb{C}^n$.

articles.title: McKay's question 16.58 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
It is not the case that a group has exactly
one irreducible complex representation of each dimension $n \ge 1$, up to equivalence, if and only
if it is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Here a representation of dimension $n$ is any
homomorphism to $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ of abstract groups, with no continuity required.

Applying a field automorphism $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{C}$ to matrix entries gives irreducible
$2$-dimensional representations $x \mapsto x^\varphi$ of the abstract group
$\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$, infinitely many of them pairwise non-equivalent (von Neumann), so
$\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$ itself lacks the property. It does have it if only unitary
representations are counted, as these are continuous (Cartan).

## Sources

- E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 16.58 (J. McKay); resolution: V. P. Burichenko, letter of 16 July 2013, as recorded in the Kourovka Archive (observation of J. von Neumann), Kourovka Archive, Problem 16.58 (No: for field automorphisms φ of ℂ the representations x ↦ x^φ of SU₂(ℂ) are irreducible and infinitely many are pairwise non-equivalent, so SU₂(ℂ) itself lacks the property; it has it for unitary representations, which are continuous by É. Cartan).

articles.title: McKay's question on $\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$ (Kourovka 16.58)
articles.statement:
A group $G$ has exactly
one irreducible complex representation of each dimension $n = 1, 2, \dots$, up to equivalence, if
and only if $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Here a representation of dimension
$n$ is any homomorphism $G \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ of abstract groups, with no continuity
required.

articles.title: Continuous semilinear representation
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a topological group, $R$ a topological
ring and $M$ a topological abelian group that is a finite free $R$-module. Suppose that $G$ acts
on $R$ by ring automorphisms and on $M$ by additive automorphisms, and that the actions of $G$ on
$R$, of $G$ on $M$ and of $R$ on $M$ are jointly continuous. This is a continuous semilinear
representation of $G$ on $M$ when $g \cdot (r x) = (g \cdot r)(g \cdot x)$ for all $g \in G$,
$r \in R$ and $x \in M$, and the coordinate map $M \to R^n$ of a fixed basis of $M$ over $R$,
where $n$ is the size of the basis, is a homeomorphism onto $R^n$ with the product topology.

## Sources

- arXiv:2608.00845, Definition `defsemilinrep` (lines 1947–1950); this class records its object-level content.

articles.title: Representations of compact groups are semisimple
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a compact topological group
and let $\rho$ be a representation of $G$ on a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$ such that
the action map $G \times V \to V$, $(g, v) \mapsto \rho(g)(v)$, is continuous. Then $\rho$ is
semisimple: every subrepresentation of $\rho$ has a complementary subrepresentation.

## Sources

- H. Weyl, *Theorie der Darstellung kontinuierlicher halb-einfacher Gruppen durch lineare Transformationen* (1925–26); Peter–Weyl (1927). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §21. Problem `compact_group_semisimple` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Peter–Weyl theorem: unitary representations separate points
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a compact Hausdorff
topological group and let $x \ne y$ be elements of $G$. Then there are an integer $n > 0$ and a
continuous map $\rho$ from $G$ to the complex $n \times n$ matrices such that $\rho(1) = 1$,
$\rho(gh) = \rho(g)\rho(h)$ for all $g, h \in G$, the matrix $\rho(g)$ is unitary for every
$g \in G$, and $\rho(x) \ne \rho(y)$.

## Sources

- F. Peter and H. Weyl, Math. Ann. 97 (1927), 737–755; Folland, A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis 2nd ed.; Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction 2nd ed.

articles.title: Schur–Weyl duality: the general linear side
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field, $M$ a finite-dimensional
vector space over $R$, and $k$ a natural number such that $k!$ is invertible in $R$. In the
algebra of $R$-linear endomorphisms of the tensor power $M^{\otimes k}$, the subalgebra generated
by the image of the diagonal action $g \mapsto g^{\otimes k}$ of $\mathrm{GL}(M)$ equals the
centralizer of the image of the action of the symmetric group $S_k$ by permuting tensor factors.

## Sources

- H. Weyl, The Classical Groups, 1939; I. Schur, Über die rationalen Darstellungen der allgemeinen linearen Gruppe, 1927. Problem `glAction_range_eq_centralizer_symAction` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Diagonal action of the general linear group on tensor powers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
semiring, $M$ an $R$-module and $k$ a natural number. Write $\mathrm{GL}(M)$ for the group of
invertible $R$-linear endomorphisms of $M$. The diagonal action of $\mathrm{GL}(M)$ on the $k$-th
tensor power $M^{\otimes k}$ is the monoid homomorphism from $\mathrm{GL}(M)$ to the
$R$-linear endomorphisms of $M^{\otimes k}$ that sends $g$ to $g^{\otimes k}$, so that
$g \cdot (v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_k) = g v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes g v_k$.

articles.title: Schur–Weyl duality: the symmetric group side
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field, $M$ a finite-dimensional
vector space over $R$, and $k$ a natural number such that $k!$ is invertible in $R$. In the
algebra of $R$-linear endomorphisms of the tensor power $M^{\otimes k}$, the subalgebra generated
by the image of the action of the symmetric group $S_k$ by permuting tensor factors equals the
centralizer of the image of the diagonal action $g \mapsto g^{\otimes k}$ of $\mathrm{GL}(M)$.

## Sources

- H. Weyl, The Classical Groups, 1939; I. Schur, Über die rationalen Darstellungen der allgemeinen linearen Gruppe, 1927. Problem `symAction_range_eq_centralizer_glAction` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Permutation action of the symmetric group on tensor powers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
semiring, $M$ an $R$-module and $k$ a natural number. The symmetric group $S_k$ of permutations of
$\{1, \dots, k\}$ acts on the $k$-th tensor power $M^{\otimes k}$ by permuting tensor factors: this
is the monoid homomorphism from $S_k$ to the $R$-linear endomorphisms of $M^{\otimes k}$ that sends
$\sigma$ to the map $v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_k \mapsto
v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)} \otimes \cdots \otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(k)}$.

articles.title: Tensor square of an irreducible $\mathfrak{e}_8$-representation of dimension $779247$
articles.statement:
There exist a complex vector space $V$ and a representation of the exceptional Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{e}_8$ over $\mathbb{C}$ on $V$ such that $V$ has dimension $779247$ over $\mathbb{C}$,
$V$ is irreducible, and the tensor square $V \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} V$, with the representation
$x \cdot (v \otimes w) = (x \cdot v) \otimes w + v \otimes (x \cdot w)$ viewed as a module over the
universal enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak{e}_8$, has exactly $40$ isotypic components.

## Sources

- Classical: representation theory of the exceptional Lie algebra e₈. Problem `e8_irrep_tensor_square_decomp` of the lean-eval benchmark.
